common_name: TexFirst Peach (Texas A&M Ultra-Low-Chill Early Yellow Peach)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in December–January while dormant; TexFirst needs only about 150–200 chill hours, letting it break dormancy reliably along the Gulf Coast where 700+ hour northern peaches bloom erratically. Self-fertile, no pollinizer required.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, spacing trees 15–20 feet apart for an open-vase canopy. TexFirst was selected at Texas A&M's College Station breeding program from open-pollinated seedlings and released for its very early ripening, yellow ground color with heavy red blush, and firm handling quality — traits that suit both dooryard and small commercial plantings in zone 8–9 Gulf gardens. Because it flowers and leafs out extremely early, site it away from low-lying frost pockets to protect the bloom from a late cold snap. Thin fruit to 4–6 inches apart within a few weeks of bloom and maintain a regular dormant-season fungicide program, since warm, humid Gulf Coast springs favor brown rot and peach leaf curl on early-ripening cultivars.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Stone Fruit Breeding Program
HortScience 47(12):1803–1805 (2012) — TexFirst, an Early-ripening, Low-chill Peach for the Subtropics

common_name: Tropic Prince Peach (Texas A&M Ultra-Low-Chill Semi-Freestone Peach)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in December–January while dormant; Tropic Prince needs only about 150 chill hours, among the lowest of any Texas A&M release, making it dependable through mild Gulf Coast winters. Self-fertile, though a second tree can improve set.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Tropic Prince naturally reaches 15–20 feet but responds well to summer pruning that keeps it at a manageable 10–12 feet for easier harvest and spraying. Ripening in late April to early May, roughly 85–90 days after bloom, the semi-freestone fruit has juicy, sweet, yellow melting flesh over a red-blushed skin. Because bloom occurs very early in the Gulf South, avoid frost-prone low ground and watch forecasts during late-winter cold snaps. Regular thinning of the heavy natural fruit set is essential to reach good fruit size, and a dormant copper spray helps manage bacterial spot and leaf curl common in humid winters.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Tropical Peach Series
University of Florida IFAS EDIS — Peach and Nectarine Varieties for Florida

common_name: Emerald Drop Pluot (Green-Skinned Low-Chill Plum-Apricot Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant bare-root in late winter; Emerald Drop needs 400 chill hours or less, within reach for zone 8b–9a Gulf gardens most winters. Not self-fertile — requires an early-blooming pollinizer such as Flavor Grenade Pluot or Santa Rosa plum planted nearby.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, siting a compatible pollinizer within 50 feet since Emerald Drop sets little fruit on its own. Bred by Floyd Zaiger, this upright, heavy-cropping tree produces medium-to-large fruit with green skin that can be picked firm and sweet in mid-summer or left to hang until it turns honey-yellow with amber flesh and a richer, more complex flavor. The long harvest window from mid-July into late August is useful for extending the pluot season in warm-winter gardens. Thin fruit early to 4–5 inches apart to prevent limb breakage under a heavy crop, and prune annually to an open center to keep the dense canopy productive.
sources: Dave Wilson Nursery — Emerald Drop Pluot Variety Notes

common_name: Flavorosa Pluot (Early Purple-Skinned Low-Chill Plum-Apricot Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant bare-root in late winter; Flavorosa needs an estimated 400–500 chill hours, achievable in most zone 8b–9a Gulf winters. Not self-fertile — plant with an early-blooming pollinizer such as Emerald Drop Pluot or Mariposa plum.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible early-blooming pollinizer nearby, since fruit set depends on cross-pollination. Flavorosa is one of the earliest-ripening Zaiger pluots, bearing medium-sized fruit with dark purple skin and juicy red flesh that carries a concentrated, plum-forward sweetness well above average brix. The moderately vigorous, spreading tree bears reliably where winter chill is on the lower end, making it a candidate for warm Gulf gardens that struggle with higher-chill plums. Thin fruit clusters to a single fruit every 4–5 inches once set to improve size, and prune to an open vase form each winter to keep the spreading habit manageable and fruit within easy reach.
sources: Dave Wilson Nursery — Flavorosa Pluot Variety Notes

common_name: Garden Annie Apricot (Self-Fertile Low-Chill Genetic Dwarf Apricot)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in December–February; Garden Annie sets a full crop after only about 300 chill hours, one of the lower requirements among named apricots and a good match for zone 8–9 Gulf winters. Self-fertile, no pollinizer needed.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil on a site with good cold-air drainage to protect the early pale-pink bloom from late frost, the main risk for any apricot in the Gulf South. Garden Annie is a genetic dwarf reaching only 8–10 feet at maturity, making it practical for smaller lots or large containers while still producing full-sized, firm, bright-yellow semi-freestone fruit that holds well on the tree through June without softening. Because it is self-fertile, a single tree will crop reliably, though hand-thinning green fruit to about 3 inches apart improves final size on this compact, densely branched tree. Watch for the shorter chill requirement to trigger occasional off-season bloom during warm winter spells, and delay heavy nitrogen feeding until after fruit set to avoid excess vegetative growth on the small frame.
sources: Willis Orchard Company — Garden Annie Apricot Variety Notes
California Rare Fruit Growers — Apricot Fruit Facts
Dave Wilson Nursery — Low-Chill Southwest Variety Recommendations
